question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
This artwork / are a wonderful example / of the period's vogue / for realistic style.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. are a wonderful example.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "This artwork", which is a singular, uncountable noun.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A singular subject must always take a singular verb. Since "artwork" is singular, the verb must be "is", not "are".
◦ Correct: This artwork is a wonderful example...
◦ Incorrect: This artwork are a wonderful example...

• The segment "are a wonderful example" therefore contains the grammatical error, because the plural verb "are" does not agree with the singular subject "artwork".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "This artwork" is correct as it is; it is simply the subject of the sentence and carries no error by itself.

• Option 2: "of the period's vogue" is grammatically correct; the possessive apostrophe with "period's" is used correctly to show the vogue belonging to the period.

• Option 3: "for realistic style" is a correctly formed prepositional phrase and contains no error.

NOTE

• Collective/abstract singular nouns like artwork, furniture, advice, information, news, luggage are always followed by a singular verb and never take a plural "-s".

• Always locate the true subject of the sentence first (ignoring intervening phrases) before deciding whether the verb should be singular or plural — this is one of the most frequently tested error-spotting patterns in SSC exams.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts. Identify the part that contains an error.
Pratigya arrived / to the / railway station / five hours early.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. to the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "arrive" takes a specific preposition depending on the type of place being referred to.

• Rule — Preposition with "arrive":
◦ Arrive at + a point/small place (station, airport, office, a specific spot).
◦ Arrive in + a large place (city, country).

• Since "railway station" is a specific point/place, the correct preposition is "at", not "to". The sentence should read: "Pratigya arrived at the railway station five hours early."

• The part "to the" therefore contains the error, as "to" is the wrong preposition to use after "arrived" here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "railway station" is a correctly formed noun phrase and contains no error.

• Option 2: "Pratigya arrived" is grammatically correct — a proper noun subject followed by the correct past tense form of "arrive".

• Option 4: "five hours early" is a correct adverbial phrase of time and contains no error.

NOTE

• Commonly confused prepositions with verbs of motion: reach + (no preposition, e.g. "reach home"), arrive at/in, get to.

• Remember: we never say "reach to" — "reach" is directly followed by the place (e.g. "He reached the station"), which is another very frequently tested SSC error.

question:
Identify the error in the following sentence and select the option with the correct use of the phrasal verb.
Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he blacked out.
option_1: Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he broke in.
option_2: Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he chickened out.
option_3: Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he checked out.
option_4: Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he turned down.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Prateek was planning to ask Shreya for a favour. But he could not muster up the courage. So, he chickened out.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "chicken out" means to withdraw from something out of fear or nervousness, to fail to do something because one loses one's nerve/courage. (डर के मारे पीछे हट जाना)
◦ Example: He was going to go bungee jumping, but he chickened out at the last moment.

• The context of the sentence — Prateek "could not muster up the courage" — clearly signals loss of nerve, which is exactly the meaning of "chickened out". The originally used phrasal verb "blacked out" (meaning to lose consciousness) does not fit this context at all.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "broke in" means to enter a place by force (as a burglar does), or to interrupt while someone is speaking — irrelevant here.

• Option 3: "checked out" means to leave a hotel after paying the bill, or informally to investigate/look at something — it does not convey loss of courage.

• Option 4: "turned down" means to reject or refuse an offer/request — this describes Shreya refusing Prateek, not Prateek losing his nerve, so it does not fit the sentence.

NOTE

• Other phrasal verbs related to courage/fear frequently asked in SSC: back out (withdraw from a commitment), buck up (become more cheerful/courageous), cave in (give in under pressure), screw up one's courage (gather courage to do something difficult).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The companies were / giving in the prizes / to attract customers / during the festive season.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. giving in the prizes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The intended meaning of the sentence is that the companies were distributing/handing out prizes to attract customers. The correct phrasal verb for this meaning is "give away", not "give in".

• Rule — Phrasal verb usage:
◦ Give away = to distribute something free of cost, to hand out.
◦ Give in = to surrender, to yield or stop resisting.

• Since the companies are distributing prizes (not surrendering), the sentence should read: "The companies were giving away the prizes to attract customers during the festive season."

• The segment "giving in the prizes" therefore contains the error, since "give in" is the wrong phrasal verb for the intended meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The companies were" is grammatically correct — a plural subject with the correct plural auxiliary "were".

• Option 3: "during the festive season" is a correctly formed prepositional phrase of time and contains no error.

• Option 4: "to attract customers" is a correct infinitive phrase showing purpose, and contains no error.

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verb pairs in SSC exams: give away vs. give in, give up (to stop doing something) vs. give out (to distribute/run out), take in (to deceive/absorb) vs. take on (to undertake).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Famines were (1) ___________ during the period of British rule due to many reasons (2) ___________ unemployment following import of machine-made goods from Britain, overexploitation of farmers and (3) __________ access to food. India suffered two very severe droughts in 1965 and 1966. India achieved (4) ___________ in food grains by the year 1976 through the implementation of the seed-water-fertiliser-led (5) ___________. The country is no longer exposed to real famines. However, lack of purchasing power continues to haunt people in some parts of the country.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. caused.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a word that logically connects with "during the period of British rule due to many reasons" — the sentence is explaining what happened to famines and why. "Caused" fits perfectly: "Famines were caused during the period of British rule due to many reasons..."

• "Excruciated" (meaning to cause intense pain) and "discouraged" are not used to describe famines being brought about, and "paused" does not fit the sense of famines being the result of causes listed afterward.

• Grammatically, the passive structure "were + past participle (caused)" fits smoothly with the following clause "due to many reasons", which explains the cause.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "excruciated" means to inflict severe pain on someone; it cannot logically follow "famines were" in this context.

• Option 3: "paused" means stopped temporarily; famines being "paused... due to many reasons" makes no logical sense.

• Option 4: "discouraged" means to be deterred/demotivated; this does not fit with "famines" as the subject.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the full sentence (not just the blank) and check which option keeps the sentence's cause-effect logic and grammatical structure intact — here, "due to many reasons" that follow the blank is the key clue pointing to "caused".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Famines were (1) ___________ during the period of British rule due to many reasons (2) ___________ unemployment following import of machine-made goods from Britain, overexploitation of farmers and (3) __________ access to food. India suffered two very severe droughts in 1965 and 1966. India achieved (4) ___________ in food grains by the year 1976 through the implementation of the seed-water-fertiliser-led (5) ___________. The country is no longer exposed to real famines. However, lack of purchasing power continues to haunt people in some parts of the country.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. including large-scale.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence lists the reasons for famines: **"...due to many reasons (2) ___________ unemployment following import of machine-made goods from Britain, overexploitation of farmers and (3) __________ access to food."**

• Since unemployment (caused by the import of machine-made goods replacing manual labour) is being cited as one of the reasons, the blank should mean "including" — i.e., the reasons include large-scale unemployment. Large-scale industrial import of machine-made goods would put large numbers of artisans/workers out of work, so "large-scale" fits better than "small-scale".

• Hence the correct phrase is "including large-scale unemployment".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "excluding large-scale" is incorrect because "excluding" would mean unemployment is NOT one of the reasons, which contradicts the sense of the passage (it is listed as a reason).

• Option 2: "excluding small-scale" is incorrect for the same reason — "excluding" reverses the intended meaning.

• Option 3: "including small-scale" is incorrect because the scale of unemployment caused by the wholesale import of British machine-made goods (replacing traditional industries) was large-scale, not small-scale.

NOTE

• "Including" vs. "excluding" is a common cloze trap in SSC exams — always check whether the listed item is being added to or removed from the set being discussed.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Famines were (1) ___________ during the period of British rule due to many reasons (2) ___________ unemployment following import of machine-made goods from Britain, overexploitation of farmers and (3) __________ access to food. India suffered two very severe droughts in 1965 and 1966. India achieved (4) ___________ in food grains by the year 1976 through the implementation of the seed-water-fertiliser-led (5) ___________. The country is no longer exposed to real famines. However, lack of purchasing power continues to haunt people in some parts of the country.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. restricted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"...overexploitation of farmers and (3) __________ access to food."** This is listing negative conditions that led to famines, so the blank must describe access to food in a negative way — i.e., access that was limited/curtailed.

• "Restricted" means limited or controlled, which fits perfectly: people had restricted (limited) access to food, contributing to famine.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "basic" access to food does not convey the negative, famine-causing sense required by the context.

• Option 3: "unlimited" access to food is the opposite of what causes famine, so it does not fit logically.

• Option 4: "inflated" describes prices or numbers, not "access"; it is not idiomatically used with "access to food".

NOTE

• When a cloze blank lists causes of a negative event (like famine), look for words with a similarly negative connotation (restricted, limited, scarce, denied) rather than neutral or positive words.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Famines were (1) ___________ during the period of British rule due to many reasons (2) ___________ unemployment following import of machine-made goods from Britain, overexploitation of farmers and (3) __________ access to food. India suffered two very severe droughts in 1965 and 1966. India achieved (4) ___________ in food grains by the year 1976 through the implementation of the seed-water-fertiliser-led (5) ___________. The country is no longer exposed to real famines. However, lack of purchasing power continues to haunt people in some parts of the country.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. self-sufficiency.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"India achieved (4) ___________ in food grains by the year 1976 through the implementation of the seed-water-fertiliser-led (5) ___________." This refers to the well-known historical fact that India achieved self-sufficiency in food grains** through the Green Revolution (the seed-water-fertiliser-led strategy) by the mid-1970s.

• "Self-sufficiency" means the ability to meet one's own needs (here, food grain needs) without depending on external help/imports — exactly what India accomplished after the Green Revolution.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "goal" does not fit grammatically or contextually with "achieved ___ in food grains" as naturally as "self-sufficiency".

• Option 2: "incompetency" means lack of ability, which is the opposite of what India achieved — this contradicts the historically positive tone of the passage.

• Option 3: "success" is a plausible-sounding general word, but it does not precisely capture the specific, well-documented historical achievement — "self-sufficiency in food grains" is the standard collocation used to describe this outcome of the Green Revolution.

NOTE

• General-awareness-linked English cloze passages in SSC often test knowledge of standard collocations tied to real facts — here, "self-sufficiency in food grains" and "Green Revolution" are fixed, commonly used phrases that should be recognised together.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Famines were (1) ___________ during the period of British rule due to many reasons (2) ___________ unemployment following import of machine-made goods from Britain, overexploitation of farmers and (3) __________ access to food. India suffered two very severe droughts in 1965 and 1966. India achieved (4) ___________ in food grains by the year 1976 through the implementation of the seed-water-fertiliser-led (5) ___________. The country is no longer exposed to real famines. However, lack of purchasing power continues to haunt people in some parts of the country.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Green Revolution.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes **"the seed-water-fertiliser-led (5) ___________" that helped India achieve self-sufficiency in food grains by 1976. This is a direct reference to the Green Revolution**, the historical agricultural movement in India based on high-yielding seed varieties, irrigation and chemical fertilisers.

• The phrase "seed-water-fertiliser-led" is the standard description of the Green Revolution strategy, making "Green Revolution" the only contextually and factually correct choice.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Blue Revolution" refers to the growth of the fisheries and aquaculture sector in India, not food grains.

• Option 2: "Pink Revolution" refers to the growth of the meat and poultry processing industry (or, in some contexts, onion production), not food grains.

• Option 4: "White Revolution" (also called Operation Flood) refers to the growth of milk production/dairy farming in India, not food grains.

NOTE

• SSC frequently tests these India-specific "Revolution" terms: Green Revolution — food grains, White Revolution — milk, Blue Revolution — fish, Yellow Revolution — oilseeds, Golden Revolution — horticulture/honey, Silver Revolution — eggs/poultry.

question:
Read the sentence carefully and select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined part.
The revolt of the labourers will be considered as an epoch in the world history.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. important period.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "epoch" means a particular period of time in history or a person's life, especially one marked by notable events or characterised as being significant. (एक महत्वपूर्ण युग/काल)
◦ Example: The invention of the internet marked a new epoch in human communication.

• In the given sentence, the revolt of the labourers is being described as marking a significant period in world history, so "important period" is the closest and most accurate substitute for "epoch".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "unpopular measure" does not match the meaning of "epoch" at all — "epoch" has nothing to do with popularity or a measure/policy.

• Option 2: "hostile event" wrongly suggests hostility/aggression, whereas "epoch" is a neutral term referring only to a marked period of time, not the nature of an event.

• Option 4: "commendable act" incorrectly implies praiseworthiness, but "epoch" carries no judgment of an act being good or praiseworthy — it simply denotes a significant time period.

NOTE

• Words related to "epoch": era (एक युग), age, milestone (turning point). Do not confuse "epoch" (a period of time) with "episode" (a single event/incident).

question:
Read the given sentence carefully. Change the meaning of the sentence by replacing the underlined word with its ANTONYM from the following options.
I have keen interest in reading the mind of those students who are boisterous at home but on their best behaviour at school.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. placid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "boisterous" means noisy, energetic, and full of unrestrained high spirits; rowdy. (शोरगुल मचाने वाला/उछल-कूद करने वाला)

• Its antonym is "placid", which means calm and peaceful, not easily upset or excited. (शांत/स्थिर)
◦ Example: Unlike her boisterous brother, she has a placid temperament.

• Replacing "boisterous" with "placid" reverses the meaning of the sentence, as required by the question.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "clamorous" means loud and noisy — this is a synonym, not an antonym, of "boisterous".

• Option 2: "frothing" means foaming, often used to describe someone extremely agitated or angry — this intensifies rather than reverses the sense of "boisterous".

• Option 4: "raucous" means harsh-sounding and disorderly — this too is a synonym of "boisterous", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "boisterous": rowdy, unruly, rambunctious, clamorous, raucous. Antonyms: placid, calm, sedate, docile, subdued.

question:
Choose the option that best describes the meaning of the idioms and phrases underlined in the given sentence.
You can best identify the fair weather friends at the time of adversity.
option_1: Friends who come in good weather conditions
option_4: Friend only at the time of prosperity
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Friend only at the time of prosperity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "fair-weather friend" means a person who is a friend only when things are going well, but who deserts you in times of trouble or difficulty. (मतलबी दोस्त, केवल सुख के समय का साथी)
◦ Example: He turned out to be a fair-weather friend — he vanished the moment I needed help.

• The sentence itself confirms this meaning by saying such friends can be "best identified... at the time of adversity" (i.e., they disappear during hard times), matching "friend only at the time of prosperity".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Friends who come in good weather conditions" is a literal, word-for-word (non-idiomatic) reading of the phrase, not its actual figurative meaning.

• Option 2: "Best friends" is incorrect, as the idiom actually describes an unreliable, self-interested friend — the opposite of a "best friend".

• Option 3: "Friends who bring good rain" is an unrelated, literal misinterpretation with no connection to the idiom's true meaning.

NOTE

• Related idioms often tested by SSC: "a friend in need is a friend indeed" (a true friend helps during hardship), "fair-weather friend" is its direct opposite.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.
I can't begin to talk on this situation right now; I am still wrapping my head around it.
option_3: Comparing two things that can't be compared
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Understanding something complicated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to wrap one's head around (something)" means to come to understand or accept a difficult or complicated idea or situation. (किसी जटिल बात को समझने की कोशिश करना)
◦ Example: It took me a while to wrap my head around the new tax rules.

• In the sentence, the speaker says they "can't begin to talk" about the situation because they are still "wrapping their head around it" — i.e., still trying to understand/process this complicated situation, matching Option 2.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Ignoring something completely" is incorrect — the idiom conveys active mental engagement with a problem, not avoidance of it.

• Option 3: "Comparing two things that can't be compared" describes a different idiom altogether (like "comparing apples and oranges"), not this one.

• Option 4: "Revealing a secret nobody knows" has no connection to the idiom's actual meaning of mental comprehension.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of understanding: "get the hang of (something)" (to learn how to do something), "get one's head round something" (British variant of the same idiom), "make sense of" (to understand something confusing).

question:
There is a spelling error in the given sentence. Select the option that contains the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
The mighty gaint brought a marigold for the princess.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. gaint.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "giant" — a mythical or legendary being of great size and strength. The word printed in the sentence, "gaint", has the letters "a" and "i" wrongly transposed.

• Spelling key: G + I + A + N + T. Remember the sequence "i" before "a" (as in the common pattern "-iant", also seen in words like "radiant" and "defiant").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "princess" is spelt correctly — a female member of a royal family.

• Option 3: "marigold" is spelt correctly — a common orange/yellow flowering plant.

• Option 4: "mighty" is spelt correctly — meaning powerful or strong.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-iant": giant, radiant, defiant, reliant, brilliant. Always check the order of vowels carefully in such words, as SSC frequently tests letter-transposition errors like "gaint" for "giant".

question:
Identify the incorrectly spelt word and select its correct spelling.
The calandar was reformed during the time of Julius Caesar.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. calandar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word printed in the sentence, "calandar", is misspelt. The correct spelling is "calendar" — a chart or system showing the days, weeks and months of a year.

• Spelling key: C + A + L + E + N + D + A + R. Note the middle letter is "e" (calendar), not "a" — a common source of confusion is with the unrelated word "calender" (a machine used to smooth/press paper or cloth), which is spelt with an "e" in the third syllable instead of "a".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "reeformed" is not the correct spelling of the intended word; the correct spelling as it should appear is "reformed" (only one "e"), but this word is spelt correctly as "reformed" in the original sentence and is not the target error here.

• Option 2: "celender" is not a word that appears in the sentence and is a distractor option.

• Option 3: "riformed" is also not a word that appears in the sentence and is a distractor option.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "calendar" (a system of dates) with "calender" (a machine for pressing/glazing paper or cloth) or "colander" (a kitchen strainer) — these three similar-sounding words are commonly tested together in SSC spelling questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Fertile
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Productive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "fertile" means (of land) able to produce a large amount of good-quality crops or vegetation; producing abundant results. (उपजाऊ)
◦ Example: The Gangetic plains are known for their fertile soil.

• "Productive" means producing or able to produce large amounts of goods, crops, or results, which closely matches the meaning of "fertile" in both literal (land) and figurative (mind/period) senses.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Destructive" means causing great damage — this is close to the opposite of "fertile" (barren land could be seen as unproductive, but "destructive" specifically means harmful, not merely unproductive).

• Option 3: "Hectic" means full of frantic activity — unrelated to the idea of productivity of land or output.

• Option 4: "Amusing" means causing laughter or providing entertainment — entirely unrelated to "fertile".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "fertile": fruitful, prolific, rich, productive, fecund. Antonyms: barren, infertile, sterile, unproductive.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Many a women work for the betterment of their family.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Many a woman works for.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — "Many a" + Noun: The structure "Many a" is always followed by a singular countable noun and a singular verb, even though the meaning conveyed is plural (i.e., "many").
◦ Structure: Many a + singular noun + singular verb
◦ Example: Many a soldier has died for the country. (NOT "many a soldiers have died")

• Applying the rule: "women" (plural) must become "woman" (singular), and the verb must be the singular present-tense form "works", not "work". The corrected phrase is: "Many a woman works for..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Many a woman worked for" wrongly changes the tense to past ("worked"), whereas the rest of the sentence remains in the present tense ("of their family" — the sentence describes a general, ongoing truth), so the verb should stay in the present.

• Option 2: "Many a women working for" incorrectly retains the plural "women" and uses the non-finite "-ing" form "working", which cannot function as the main verb of the sentence.

• Option 4: "Many a women works for" incorrectly retains the plural noun "women" even though the verb "works" has correctly been made singular — the noun and verb must both follow the "many a" rule.

NOTE

• Similar fixed structures that take a singular noun + singular verb despite implying plurality: "many a time", "more than one" (e.g., "more than one student was present").

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the sentence.
He purchased very cheap dresses.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Expensive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "cheap" means low in price; costing little money. (सस्ता)

• Its direct antonym is "expensive", meaning costing a lot of money. (महंगा)
◦ Example: She prefers buying expensive dresses from designer boutiques rather than cheap ones.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Doltish" means stupid or foolish — this describes a person's intelligence, not price, and is unrelated to "cheap".

• Option 3: "Lively" means full of energy and enthusiasm — this describes character/mood, not price, and is unrelated.

• Option 4: "Paltry" means very small or meagre in amount/value — this is actually close in meaning to "cheap" (a synonym, e.g. "a paltry sum"), not its antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "cheap": inexpensive, economical, affordable, paltry (of amounts), low-cost. Antonyms: expensive, costly, dear, pricey.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
He is almost quiet well.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. quite.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The words "quite" and "quiet" are commonly confused because they look and sound similar, but they have entirely different meanings and grammatical roles.

• Rule — quite vs. quiet:
◦ Quite (adverb) = completely, fairly, or to a certain extent; used to intensify an adjective (e.g., "quite well", "quite good").
◦ Quiet (adjective) = making little or no noise; calm, silent.

• In the given sentence, "well" here means "in good health" (an adjective), and it needs a degree adverb before it — the correct, natural expression is "He is quite well" (i.e., he is completely/fairly healthy). The word "almost" is redundant, and "quiet" is the wrong word altogether, since silence has no connection to being in good health.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "almost quietly" wrongly retains "quiet" (as its adverb form "quietly"), which is unrelated to the intended meaning of good health.

• Option 2: "quiet" alone ("He is quiet well") is grammatically odd and still uses the wrong word "quiet" instead of the required "quite".

• Option 3: "very quite" is incorrect because "quite" is already a degree adverb and cannot be further modified by another degree adverb like "very" in standard usage — "very quite" is not idiomatic English.

NOTE

• "Quite" + adjective = to a considerable/complete extent (quite good, quite well, quite sure). "Quiet" is always about the absence of noise/disturbance (a quiet room, a quiet child). This spelling/usage confusion is a favourite SSC trap.

question:
Complete the given sentence with an appropriate homophone from the given options.
It is better to focus on your __________ than to wander aimlessly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. career.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word meaning "a person's course or progress through life, especially in a profession/occupation", which is exactly the meaning of "career" — correctly spelt as C-A-R-E-E-R.

• The sentence "It is better to focus on your career than to wander aimlessly" makes complete sense with this meaning — advising someone to concentrate on their professional path rather than drift without direction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "carrier" means a person or thing that carries/transports something (e.g., a mail carrier, disease carrier) — it does not fit the context of focusing on one's life/profession.

• Option 2: "courier" means a person or company employed to deliver messages/packages — again unrelated to the intended meaning here.

• Option 4: "carreer" is simply a misspelling of "career" (with an extra "r") and is not a correctly spelt English word.

NOTE

• "Career", "carrier" and "courier" are commonly confused near-homophones in SSC exams. Remember: career = profession/life path; carrier = one who carries/transports; courier = delivery person/service.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to correct the sentence by using the meaning of the underlined word.
In the winter season, the poor woman needed a refuge where she could live freely and independently.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Shelter.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "refuge" means a condition of being safe or sheltered from pursuit, danger, or trouble; a place providing shelter or protection. (शरण/आश्रय स्थल)
◦ Example: During the storm, the villagers took refuge in the community hall.

• The sentence describes a poor woman needing a safe place to stay during winter where she could live on her own — this is best captured by the general meaning of "shelter", which directly corresponds to "refuge".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "School" is an educational institution and has no connection to the meaning of "refuge" (a place of safety/shelter).

• Option 3: "Inn" specifically refers to a small commercial hotel or public house, which is a narrower and more specific concept than the general protective shelter conveyed by "refuge", and also implies payment rather than a free place of safety.

• Option 4: "Tent" refers to a specific type of temporary portable structure, which is far too narrow and specific compared to the broader meaning of "refuge" as any place of safety/shelter.

NOTE

• Words related to "refuge": sanctuary (a safe/protected place), asylum (protection granted, especially to political refugees), haven (a place of safety).

question: The balloon started to deflate after being pricked with a needle. What is the ANTONYM of 'deflate'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Inflate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "deflate" means to let air or gas out of something (such as a tyre or balloon), causing it to become smaller or flatter. (हवा निकालना/पिचकाना)

• Its direct antonym is "inflate", meaning to fill something with air or gas so that it expands. (हवा भरना/फुलाना)
◦ Example: He used a pump to inflate the flat tyre.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Flatten" means to make something flat or level — this is actually a synonym, not an antonym, of "deflate" (a deflated object becomes flat).

• Option 2: "Compress" means to press or squeeze something into a smaller space — this too is close in meaning to "deflate" (reducing size/volume), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Shrink" means to become smaller in size — again, this describes the same effect as deflation, not its opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "deflate": flatten, compress, shrink, collapse, let down. Antonyms: inflate, expand, swell, distend, pump up.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Affirm
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Confirm.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "affirm" means to state something positively and with confidence; to declare firmly and publicly that something is true. (दृढ़तापूर्वक पुष्टि करना)
◦ Example: The witness affirmed that she had seen the accused at the scene.

• "Confirm" means to establish the truth or correctness of something, to state something with certainty, which closely matches the meaning of "affirm".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Convey" means to communicate or make known an idea/feeling — it does not carry the specific sense of asserting something is true.

• Option 3: "Correlate" means to have a mutual relationship between two or more things — this is unrelated to declaring something true.

• Option 4: "Deliver" means to bring or hand something over, or to give a speech — unrelated to the meaning of firmly asserting truth.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "affirm": assert, declare, confirm, verify, testify. Antonyms: deny, negate, refute, contradict.

question:
Select the most appropriate homophone to fill in the blank.
The mechanics tried a lot to get that car __________ from the accident spot.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. towed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word meaning "pulled/dragged behind a vehicle using a rope or chain", which is exactly the meaning of "towed" (past tense of "tow").

• The sentence "The mechanics tried a lot to get that car towed from the accident spot" makes complete sense — the mechanics were trying to pull the damaged car away using another vehicle.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "told" means to have communicated information — this does not fit the physical action of moving a car and is not even a homophone of "towed".

• Option 3: "toed" relates to "toe" (a digit of the foot), as in "toed the line" — it is a near-homophone but does not fit the meaning required here.

• Option 4: "toad" refers to an amphibian animal — a homophone of "towed" in some accents, but completely unrelated in meaning to moving a car.

NOTE

• "Towed", "toed" and "toad" are commonly grouped homophones in SSC exams. Remember: tow = to pull a vehicle; toe = a digit of the foot; toad = an amphibian.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word segment in the following sentence.
It is a high-pay job.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. high-paying.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The compound adjective "high-pay" is not a grammatically standard form to describe a job before the noun "job". A job that offers a high salary is correctly described using the present-participle compound adjective "high-paying".

• Rule — Compound adjectives with jobs/salaries: When describing a job/position that offers a high or low salary, English uses the "-paying" form (the job actively "pays" a certain amount): a high-paying job, a low-paying job. The "-paid" form (past participle) is instead used to describe the person who receives the salary: a highly paid executive, an underpaid worker.

• Since the sentence describes the job itself (not a person), the correct form is "high-paying": "It is a high-paying job."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "low-paid" is incorrect on two counts — it reverses the meaning from "high" to "low", and it wrongly uses the "-paid" form with "job" instead of "-paying".

• Option 3: "high-paid" keeps the correct meaning "high" but incorrectly uses the past-participle form "-paid" with "job"; "-paid" more naturally describes a person (e.g., "a highly paid employee"), not the job itself.

• Option 4: "low-pay" is incorrect as it both reverses the meaning to "low" and retains the ungrammatical bare-noun form "pay" instead of the required "-paying" adjective form.

NOTE

• Similar "-ing" vs. "-ed" compound adjective pairs frequently tested by SSC: a well-paying job vs. a well-paid employee, a time-consuming task (the task consumes time) vs. a bored student (the student feels boredom).
